bps_operationalization_summary: The model is operationalized as a clinician-facing review framework: age-specific pathophysiology, precision diagnostics, pharmacology/de-prescribing, non-pharmacological interventions, psychological therapies, and multidisciplinary care. It defines BPS pain as peripheral nociception, central processing, and psychological state, then maps interventions to those domains rather than testing a three-domain causal model.

Social factors mainly alter access to psychological care and multidisciplinary implementation; no full three-domain causal mechanism is specified.

conceptual_tensions: MPS is framed both as a localized myofascial condition with trigger points and as a complex geriatric syndrome rooted in aging biology; The review advocates a geroscience-informed mechanistic cascade but states that interactions among aging mechanisms remain largely theoretical; Digital therapeutics are promoted for access, while the digital divide is identified as a barrier to equitable uptake; Multidisciplinary care is idealized, but the case example shows missing psychology and social work in China/resource-limited settings; Non-pharmacological care is prioritized, but pharmacological precision prescribing and de-prescribing remain necessary
additional_observations: The review prioritizes high-quality evidence but uses a narrative thematic synthesis, not a pooled meta-analysis or formal systematic review; The social domain is mostly implementation/access: digital divide, family support, social determinants, and care-team composition; The clinical case is used rhetorically and illustratively, not analyzed as empirical data; Several citation placeholders are blank in the supplied text, so attribution is sometimes unresolvable; The framework is actionable for clinicians but not empirically validated as a model
synthesis_note: This narrative review operationalizes BPS as a clinician-facing multimodal framework for geriatric MPS. Biological geroscience mechanisms are the strongest thread; psychological constructs and therapies are integrated mechanistically with central sensitization; social factors enter mainly as access, support, and care-system gaps. It offers descriptive triadic integration but few tested cross-domain pathways.
coding_rationale: Biological and psychological content are elaborated; social content is mentioned. Bio-psych integration is mechanistic, triadic integration descriptive. Typology true_integrative despite thin social domain.

conceptual_tensions: PNE is framed as biopsychosocial, but much of the operational content is biological pain education, so social and psychological domains enter mainly as determinants of acceptance; Brain-based pain explanations may reduce tissue-damage beliefs, yet the review reports they can make pain seem invented or psychological; Clinicians recognize psychological factors, but the paper finds limited tools, confidence, training, and professional culture barriers to addressing them; Group PNE is described as motivating and supportive, but also potentially tiring, hard to remember, and not suitable for all patients; The paper calls for mechanistic work on clinician–patient relationship, but explicitly notes a lack of experimental evidence for that relationship
additional_observations: The review is not a direct test of BPS as a model, it is a review of determinants of PNE acceptance; The BPS label appears in inclusion criteria, but the synthesis organizes findings as facilitators/barriers rather than as domains with specified interactions; Included studies were adult chronic musculoskeletal pain patients and healthcare providers from multiple countries and care levels; The review excludes pediatric, postsurgical, cancer-related, and pregnancy-related chronic pain; PNE variants include video, booklets, metaphors, in-person sessions, group sessions, individualized sessions, and multimodal PNE+; The paper relies heavily on qualitative determinants and cites experimental evidence only selectively in the discussion
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly as the content and scope of PNE rather than as a tested explanatory model. Biological and psychological material is central; social factors are mostly implementation determinants. It lists domains and determinants, but does not model a three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: BPS is used as an organizing/operational frame for PNE; all three domains appear, but mainly as parallel determinants of acceptance. Mechanistic pairwise links are noted, especially trust–neural activity, so triadic integration is partial.

conceptual_tensions: The paper uses a broad BPS frame while not defining the model itself; Biological and psychological evidence is detailed, but socioeconomic evidence rests mainly on one education study; Pain sensitization, neuropathic-like pain, and catastrophizing overlap, and adjustment changes associations; Many reported associations are inconsistent across observational studies; Clinical implications extend to preoperative opioid reduction and digital adherence support even though some were excluded or not included
additional_observations: Meta-analysis was not conducted because of heterogeneity and limited studies per category; All included studies were observational cohort designs, resulting in low overall quality; The review distinguishes modifiable from non-modifiable risk factors for prehabilitation and informed consent; Some included studies also included knee or shoulder arthroplasty but required separate THA data; The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' to organize risk-factor extraction and clinical recommendations rather than to define variables in a single predictive model
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS as a structured inventory of preoperative predictors for CPSP after THA. Biological and psychological factors are developed in detail; socioeconomic factors are mentioned but evidence is thin; lifestyle implications are added in discussion. It proposes no cross-domain mechanism and mostly links domains as associated risk factors.
coding_rationale: BPS is primarily an organizing/intervention frame. Bio and psych are elaborated, social and lifestyle mentioned, spiritual absent. Triadic integration is descriptive, not mechanistic.

conceptual_tensions: BPS language is used to support self-management, but the paper does not turn the model into measured variables or a triadic mechanism; Self-management is described as multimodal, yet the heterogeneity of components makes it difficult to attribute effects to specific parts; Evidence is reported as beneficial, but certainty is often low or very low and methodological concerns are frequent; Patient education, behavioural therapy and CBT are sometimes grouped as psychological interventions, creating conceptual overlap; Quality of life and adverse effects are recommended as important outcomes but are less often reported in the included reviews
additional_observations: No psychological instruments are named for constructs such as kinesiophobia, pain catastrophising, coping or CBT outcomes; DC/TMD and RDC/TMD are used as diagnostic classification systems, not as measures of biopsychosocial constructs; Included systematic reviews were conducted in seven countries, but no country-specific social mechanisms are analysed; The paper does not name family, cultural, socioeconomic, compensation, stigma, or social determinant factors; Future research recommendations emphasize children and adolescents, quality of life, and adverse effects; The review reports 53% overlap of primary studies across included systematic reviews
synthesis_note: The paper uses BPS mainly to justify patient-centred, multimodal self-management for TMD. Biological content is mostly TMD anatomy, pain/function outcomes and jaw exercises; psychological content is education/behavioural/CBT and related constructs. Social content is limited to demographics, healthcare professionals and patient-centred framing. It does not propose a three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: Multifactorial typology: all domains appear, but social content is thin and cross-domain claims are mostly intervention-based rather than mechanistic.

conceptual_tensions: The review treats chronic primary and chronic secondary pain together while also noting that mechanisms and contextual challenges may differ across the two; The paper emphasizes social and systemic determinants but states that evidence on many proposed mechanisms remains limited or indirect; Gender-affirming care is framed as potentially protective while some practices such as chest binding, tucking, packing, and voice training are also described as capable of causing localized pain or strain; The review calls for longitudinal and mechanistic research because direct chronic pain endpoints have not been studied for pubertal suppression or subsequent GAHT; Intersex youth are conceptually relevant to sex characteristics and gender diversity but are explicitly outside the review's scope
additional_observations: The review's BPS operationalization is primarily narrative synthesis and clinical framing rather than a coded or measured BPS framework; The review cites mechanisms such as central sensitization, HPA-axis dysregulation, inflammatory processes, and shared neural circuits as cross-domain bridges; The paper includes lifestyle behaviors only as consequences of gender dysphoria-related avoidance, not as a developed lifestyle domain; Spiritual or existential content appears only within an intersectional list of systems shaping stress and resources; The paper uses the BPS label both analytically and rhetorically, especially in the conclusion where it recommends biopsychosocial care
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses biopsychosocial framing to organize chronic pain in transgender and gender-diverse youth around neurobiological vulnerabilities, psychosocial distress, and societal/systemic barriers. It proposes multiple cross-domain mechanisms, especially through minority stress, HPA-axis dysregulation, inflammation, and central sensitization, but it does not operationalize BPS into measured constructs or a formal model.
coding_rationale: All three core domains are elaborated and linked through stress physiology, pain sensitivity, and care barriers; lifestyle and spiritual content are mentioned only briefly. The typology is true_integrative because the paper relates all domains, though not with a fully specified unified mechanism.

integration_mechanism_summary: Psychosocial factors can set or alter CNS plasticity, descending modulation, nociceptive pathways, and musculoskeletal tissue properties; genetic and epigenetic factors modify these processes; favorable or adverse mixes set adaptive or maladaptive CNS states and sensorimotor outcomes. No single mediator is named for all three domains.

conceptual_tensions: TOPSMI is presented as more comprehensive and mechanistic, yet the authors state it may be difficult to formally test as a whole because many factors are involved; The review extends spinal-system evidence to orofacial pain while repeatedly noting that comparable orofacial datasets are much more limited; The BPS label brings in sociocultural factors, but the social evidence is thinner than the biological and psychological evidence; Management is recommended as customized to individual factor mixtures, but the paper does not provide a formal measurement or coding scheme for those mixtures; Prior theories are criticized for lacking a full picture, while TOPSMI is defended as mechanistic despite limited direct testing
additional_observations: The paper does not report formal quality assessment or risk-of-bias tools for the evidence it reviews; The main operationalization is theoretical: favorable versus adverse mix and weighting of factors sets CNS plasticity state; No named psychological instruments, pain outcome instruments, or psychosocial measurement scales are reported; The review proposes future longitudinal neuroimaging trials, biopsychosocial stratification, and gene-environment interaction models
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly through TOPSMI rather than through measured constructs. It gives rich biological and psychological mechanisms and a weaker sociocultural layer, so it operationalizes BPS mainly through TOPSMI rather than through measured constructs.
coding_rationale: TOPSMI is mechanistic triadic despite thin social evidence; biological content dominates, and no formal quality/risk tools or instruments are used.

conceptual_tensions: The BPS label is used, but the substantive integration is mainly psychological-neurobiological while social content is mostly clinical implementation; FIA is proposed as a mechanism, yet the authors repeatedly state that evidence is correlational and causal pathways are unestablished; Flow is distinguished from distraction and mindfulness, but it shares attentional and affective features with both; Direct flow-pain evidence is sparse, while indirect evidence from VR, music, arts, sports, and rehabilitation is used to support the hypothesis; Flow interventions are framed as beneficial, but barriers such as depression, cognitive impairment, low motivation, and excessive immersion are also named
additional_observations: Formal quality or bias assessment was not performed, consistent with the conceptual narrative design; The review is not a meta-analysis, approximately 40 conceptually relevant studies were qualitatively synthesized; Pain conditions are broad and include fibromyalgia, musculoskeletal pain, neuropathic pain, rehabilitation cohorts, and acute experimental pain paradigms; The biopsychosocial model is invoked but not formally defined; Operationalization occurs mainly through proposed future flow measures rather than measured constructs across all BPS domains; Social content centers on access, training, clinics, adherence, and therapeutic alliance rather than socioeconomic, cultural, or structural determinants
synthesis_note: This review uses BPS mainly as a framing label while operationalizing FIA as a psychological-neurobiological pathway. Social content is mostly implementation and access, not social determinants. It offers mechanistic bio-psych links and partial psych-social/bio-social links, but not a true triadic model.
coding_rationale: Dyadic bio-psych focus; social domain is named but thin. FIA proposes mechanisms, yet causal evidence and triadic integration remain limited.

conceptual_tensions: The paper uses BPS language to justify individualized care while the actual meta-analysis is dominated by physical outcomes and only a few psychosocial measures; External load is theoretically framed as graded exposure, but the included evidence rarely reports psychosocial outcomes and shows no clear psychosocial between-group advantage; Clinical interpretation emphasizes meaning, therapeutic alliance, and individual experience, but these elements are not operationalized in the review; Statistical significance in pain is separated from clinical relevance because the ETP pain effect did not exceed the MCID; High heterogeneity and incomplete intervention reporting limit the review's ability to test dose-response or biopsychosocial mechanisms
additional_observations: The BPS label is used mainly as a concluding rationale for individualized exercise, not as an operational model for social variables; Psychosocial variables are secondary outcomes, and PCS and TSK are scarcely reported; The Pain Monitoring Model is used only to categorize baseline pain intensity for subgroup analysis; The Fitness-Fatigue model is invoked only to interpret delayed maximal strength effects; Language restrictions and RCT filters may limit generalizability
synthesis_note: This review uses BPS mainly as a concluding rationale for individualized, contextually framed exercise. It operationalizes biology through load-related physical outcomes and psychology through a few psychosocial measures; social content is named but not measured. conceptual_tensions: The paper argues for fascia as a central peripheral driver while also insisting that fascia should not be viewed in isolation; It uses a biopsychosocial frame but gives much more substantive attention to fascia and central sensitization than to social factors; It proposes psychosocial factors amplify pain through neuroimmune and central pathways but does not elaborate the psychosocial mechanism; It criticizes muscle-centric and central sensitization models as incomplete, while proposing fascia as a unifying substrate that may risk reductionism if psychosocial domains are ignored
additional_observations: The article is a conceptual narrative review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis, despite searching PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Google Scholar; The review's most concrete operationalization is a named integrative conceptual model with fascial pathology, muscular dysfunction, central sensitization, and psychosocial influences; Psychological and social constructs are named but not measured, defined, or linked to specific instruments; The social domain is essentially collapsed into psychosocial factors, with no named social determinants such as work, family, healthcare access, or socioeconomic position
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS as a fascia-centered explanatory frame for MPS. Biological content is rich and sustained, especially fascia, nociception, inflammation, mechanotransduction, and central sensitization. Psychological content is present but mostly listed and undifferentiated. Social content is thin and underexplored. The paper proposes peripheral-to-central and neuroimmune pathways, but triadic integration remains partial rather than a fully specified three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: Bio-dominant pseudo-BPS: BPS is used analytically to organize fascia, muscle, neural, and psychosocial content, but social factors are minimally specified and triadic integration is mostly parallel with some peripheral-to-central mechanisms.

conceptual_tensions: BPS is used to justify social-factor inclusion, but the review’s own synthesis is mainly descriptive classification rather than mechanism; Biological or psychological factors are reclassified as social when socially shaped, creating a debatable boundary between domains; Social relationships are described as important for recovery, yet family and professional support remain underexplored; Social factors are often treated as adjustment variables or economic impacts rather than explanatory contributors to CLBP progression; Western WEIRD restriction may underrepresent marginalized populations and systemic or cultural injustice
additional_observations: The review explicitly states that included studies used a BPS model, but its own synthesis is a descriptive classification of social factors; No critical appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment was conducted because the authors judged it inappropriate for the scoping-review aim; The review says its reclassification of biological or psychological factors as social is descriptive and does not reinterpret original findings; The paper recommends mixed methods and participatory action research for underrepresented domains; The review calls for hypothesis-driven research to test temporal and potentially causal links between social factors and CLBP evolution
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly as a social lens for CLBP. It elaborates social and psychosocial factors, mentions biological/lifestyle factors when socially shaped, and uses BPS to justify classification and care strategies. It names pairwise pathways, especially social-psychological mediators, but does not model a three-domain system.
coding_rationale: Social-dominant pseudo-BPS: BPS organizes the review and care rationale, but biological content is thin and triadic integration is absent.

conceptual_tensions: BPS is presented as biomedical, psychological, and social, yet the review argues that prior BPS-oriented research has neglected the social; The social is criticized for being subsumed under psychosocial and psychological meanings, but the review still uses psychological constructs within social explanations; Quantitative social-factor studies are said to be limited because they focus on objective, measurable factors rather than subtle interactions and patient experience; Gender is treated both as biological sex and as gender relations/social inequality, and the review privileges the latter; The review excludes studies that discuss the social merely as an individual psychosocial phenomenon, so psychological material appears but is not analyzed as a psychological domain
additional_observations: The review’s inclusion criteria explicitly excluded studies that discussed the social merely as an individual psychosocial phenomenon from a psychological perspective; The paper states that it focused exclusively on study results related to social dimensions and did not analyze additional results from included studies; Included studies were worldwide but concentrated in Anglo-American countries, English and German language limits are named as limitations; Implications include social workers in medical teams, gender and discrimination sensitivity training, childcare options, poverty programs, housing, secure jobs, and health infrastructure; The paper treats lifestyle factors as an eighth social dimension rather than as a separate lifestyle framework
synthesis_note: This paper contributes a rich social-domain ontology of chronic pain development but not a biopsychosocial integration model. It operationalizes BPS by critiquing the neglect of social dimensions and synthesizing eight social categories; biomedical and psychological content remain background rather than mechanistically integrated.
coding_rationale: Social content is elaborated; bio, psych, and lifestyle are mentioned. BPS is used critically to justify a social-domain review, not as a three-domain mechanism.

conceptual_tensions: The BPS label frames chronic pain as biological, psychological, and social, but the review’s operational exposure is social support rather than all three domains; Social support generally appears beneficial, but spousal responses can be associated with worse pain, disability, and depression; The evidence base is mostly cross-sectional and correlational, yet the paper discusses possible causality and future longitudinal designs; Different social support constructs and questionnaires create inconsistency and obscure whether PSS, SSS, and SpR have comparable meanings; Spousal responses are explicitly not a measure of social support per se, yet they are included as an important chronic-pain social factor
additional_observations: The review does not perform meta-analysis, it uses vote counting and correlation/regression direction because of heterogeneity and lack of effect sizes; No included studies were randomized, and only eight of 40 final studies were longitudinal; Spousal responses are treated as a social exposure because they influence pain behaviour and well-being, even though the paper says they are not social support per se; The paper’s closest triadic mechanism is stress-buffering through stress appraisal and active coping, but it is not tied to a full BPS operational model; Biological content is concentrated in pain/nociception definitions and pain outcomes rather than mechanisms such as inflammation, genetics, imaging, or peripheral sensitization; The conclusion recommends spouse education and including spouses in treatment sessions, which turns social support findings into applied pain-management suggestions
synthesis_note: This review uses a BPS-labeled title/intro but operationalizes social support rather than the full BPS model. It codes PSS, SSS, and SpR against pain, QoL, depression, and anxiety, mostly with cross-sectional correlations. It offers stress-buffering and operant-learning pathways but no full biological-psychological-social system.
coding_rationale: Social support dominates; psychological outcomes are developed; biological content is limited to pain/nociception. BPS frames the topic but does not create a triadic mechanism, so pseudo_bps/partial integration.

conceptual_tensions: The article treats BPPV as benign and paroxysmal while focusing on chronic multi-canalicular presentations; The BPS label is used to critique misclassification, but the review's own causal account is vestibular-biological; Many symptom links are deductive, inductive, or abductive, with abductive sections relying on personal experience and uncertainty; Symptoms overlap with vestibular migraine, ME/CFS, WAD, and Menière's disease, making attribution difficult; The review narrows objective findings to vestibular findings rather than treating lack of findings as lack of findings generally
additional_observations: The paper's evidence synthesis method is deductive, inductive, and abductive rather than a BPS domain matrix; The Dizziness Handicap Inventory is the only named patient-reported outcome instrument; Psychological content is limited to cognitive/affective states, anxiety, stress, frustration, and quality of life; Social content is limited to diagnosis, clinicians, physiotherapy clinics, and multiple specialists; The BPS label appears only in the abstract and introduction; The review does not report a formal risk-of-bias or quality assessment tool for included studies
synthesis_note: This review uses BPS language to argue that chronic mc-BPPV symptoms are mislabeled psychosocial when vestibular findings are absent. Its operational content is vestibular neurophysiology and symptom attribution; psychological and social material is incidental. It does not develop a three-domain model or mechanism.
coding_rationale: BPS is explicit but undefined and only rhetorical/critical. Biology dominates; psych/social are thin. Triadic integration is partial because diagnostic context and affective responses are present but not mechanistically linked.

conceptual_tensions: The article frames pain as biopsychosocial but operationalizes most of the argument through lifestyle medicine, telemedicine access, and reimbursement barriers; Integrative care is presented as comprehensive, while interventional pain medicine is justified by anatomical and neurochemical pathways and rapid analgesia; Lifestyle medicine is described as evidence-based and beneficial, but constrained by time, training, adherence, resources, and insurance coverage; Telemedicine is presented as a solution to time and access barriers but itself has technical, physical-exam, tool-access, and security limitations; The paper names future outcome measures but does not specify instruments or validated measures for the constructs it discusses
additional_observations: The article is a debate rather than a systematic review or empirical study, so no quality assessment or risk-of-bias tools are reported; The paper’s strongest integration is within the biological-psychological interface, especially stress, sleep, inflammation, and substance use; Social content is substantial but mainly concerns access, support, insurance, reimbursement, policy, and telemedicine, not interpersonal mechanisms in pain care; The paper treats telemedicine as an implementation infrastructure rather than as a psychological, biological, or social construct
synthesis_note: This paper uses the biopsychosocial label to justify lifestyle medicine for chronic pain, but its substantive content is dominated by lifestyle, biomedical, and healthcare-system factors. Psychological content appears mainly as stress, anxiety, fatigue, mental health, adherence, and behavioral change. It offers some biological-psychological and social-psychological pathways, but not a full three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: BPS is explicit but mostly organizational. Lifestyle medicine supplies the operational content, with elaborated biological, lifestyle, and social domains, mentioned psychological content, and partial triadic integration.

conceptual_tensions: The review invokes a comprehensive BPS model but does not define it or use it to select, measure, or model variables; Prevalence heterogeneity is attributed to diagnostic criteria, cutoffs, and assessment tools, yet these sources of variation are not modeled; Narrative associations between sociodemographic features and CP are not statistically significant in meta-regression; European coverage is uneven, with many countries explicitly listed as missing despite the review's European scope; The discussion broadens from BPS to psychosomatic medicine, clinimetrics, macro-analysis, and Whipple's principle without resolving the BPS operational gap
additional_observations: The meta-regression operationalizes sociodemographic moderators only as sex, marital status, and employment status; Quality assessment focused on prevalence-study methods rather than BPS construct validity; SF-36 was the only named patient-reported outcome instrument in the evidence; Psychosomatic medicine, clinimetrics, macro-analysis, and Whipple's principle extend the care rationale beyond BPS; Environmental factors are named but not operationalized; Pain location and regional pain burden are the main biological operationalization
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS only as a rationale for comprehensive, multimodal care after a prevalence-focused synthesis. It names biological, psychological, and social correlates but treats them mainly as associated features, with no substantive three-domain model or measured BPS variables.
coding_rationale: Multifactorial: all domains are named, but BPS is used mainly for care recommendations. Triadic integration is descriptive only; no three-domain mechanism is modeled.

integration_mechanism_summary: PIPT combines cognitive skill training with aerobic activity, therapeutic exercise, and graded functional movement. The proposed pathway is active cognitive and physical coping behaviors, mediated by psychological flexibility, self-efficacy, reduced catastrophizing/fear/maladaptive beliefs, leading to less pain/disability and greater work/social participation. Sociocultural factors are proposed as moderators/mediators and tailoring guides, not a fully specified three-domain mechanism.

conceptual_tensions: The paper critiques existing biopsychosocial/PIPT frameworks for missing socioeconomic, ethnocultural, and interpersonal factors while proposing a PIPT model that remains centered on physical therapy interventions; The general model is grounded in PIPT evidence, yet the authors state that mediators may differ in CALD populations and must be tested; Social factors are central to tailoring and proposed as mediators/moderators, but the core mechanism remains primarily cognitive-emotional and physical; The paper calls for culturally relevant care while acknowledging that existing rehabilitation frameworks are vague, difficult to test, and limited to behavioral mechanisms; Prayer and remedios are incorporated as culturally relevant coping options alongside evidence-based PIPT techniques
additional_observations: This is a perspective/intervention logic model, not an empirical test of the proposed mechanisms; The Latino example is operationalized in a Federally Qualified Health Center near the United States-Mexico border; The social domain is more developed than in many PIPT papers but functions mainly as tailoring, moderator, mediator, and contextual determinant; The paper does not provide formal definitions for most psychological constructs beyond psychological flexibility; The article reports no quality-of-evidence appraisal because of its scoping/narrative nature; No spiritual/religious framework is developed, prayer is treated as a coping option rather than a formal construct
synthesis_note: The paper operationalizes BPS as a PIPT logic model: physical therapy components plus cognitive-emotional skill training plus sociocultural tailoring. It goes beyond listing domains by specifying mediators/moderators and culturally relevant constructs, but the social domain mainly functions as context/tailoring for a biopsychosocial PIPT mechanism rather than as an independently modeled causal system.
coding_rationale: All three domains are present and linked, but the social domain is mostly a moderator/tailoring layer; therefore triadic integration is partial rather than a fully specified three-way mechanism.

conceptual_tensions: The review proposes neuroinflammation/affect mechanisms while stating evidence is limited and attribution speculative; Exercise is framed as beneficial, yet acute bouts can worsen pain/fatigue and drive fear avoidance/adherence problems; The review focuses on older adults but notes many included participants were young and middle-aged adults; Social factors are invoked through barriers and disparities but are not measured or integrated into the main mechanism; Scoping review methods included all available literature and did not weight conclusions by quality despite risk-of-bias assessments
additional_observations: No named psychological or social instruments are used, outcomes are reported as study outcomes; The conceptual framework is central but is proposed for future testing rather than tested in this review; The paper treats exercise as both lifestyle behavior and intervention component; It distinguishes neuroinflammation from systemic inflammation but uses both in mechanisms; It calls for qualitative approaches to exercise adherence; Quality assessments were conducted but not weighted in the scoping review synthesis
synthesis_note: The review operationalizes BPS mainly through exercise, affect, neuroinflammation, and adherence in older adults with FM. It develops biological and psychological mechanisms while social factors remain barriers/context, yielding partial BPS integration.
coding_rationale: Bio and psych are elaborated; social is thin. BPS label organizes the review and supports exercise rationale, but no model definition or full triadic integration is provided.

conceptual_tensions: The paper uses a broad chronic-disease wearable frame while chronic pain is represented by only 6 of 79 studies; The BPS label is used to describe outcome categories, but no formal biopsychosocial model or chronic-pain mechanism is provided; The review reports measured outcomes and effect direction but does not consider effect sizes; Multicomponent behavioral strategy interventions are acknowledged as confounding factors but not considered; MMAT quality assessment is reported, but no studies are excluded based on MMAT scores
additional_observations: Chronic pain studies used only wearable activity trackers and reported clinical, behavioral, and technology-experience outcomes; Most included studies were conducted in North America, especially the United States; Wearable activity trackers were the most common device across the review; The paper's BPS-related content appears mainly in outcome categorization rather than in chronic-pain theory; The review includes chronic disease self-management broadly, not only pain populations; Quality assessment was performed, but methodological rigor did not determine inclusion
synthesis_note: This paper contributes a scoping map of wearable-device interventions across chronic diseases, with chronic pain as a small cluster. It operationalizes BPS only by adding a holistic/biopsychosocial outcome category; it does not define the model or propose chronic-pain-specific mechanisms. Most evidence is clinical/behavioral, with social content limited to health-care system outcomes.
coding_rationale: BPS is used as an outcome taxonomy across chronic diseases, not a chronic-pain BPS model. Bio and psych outcomes dominate; social appears mainly as health-care system outcomes. Integration is device-feedback rather than three-domain chronic-pain mechanism.

conceptual_tensions: The paper says BPS requires interaction of physical, emotional and social factors, but the substantive review is mainly psychosocial implementation with biological factors mostly listed; Screening tools for psychosocial risk are recommended in musculoskeletal care, yet orthopaedics lacks a universal comprehensive patient interview incorporating a biopsychosocial approach; Decision aids are presented as shared decision-making tools, but the paper says decision aids without interactive processes have not improved surgical outcomes; Multidisciplinary mental health care is recommended, but workforce costs and funding models are barriers; Equity is emphasized for women and culturally diverse communities, but the paper says these groups have been excluded from research previously
additional_observations: The article is a state-of-the-art implementation review, not an effectiveness synthesis of BPS interventions; It uses primary-care musculoskeletal evidence to infer what orthopaedic surgery should implement; It treats psychosocial assessment as a screening and implementation task rather than as a validated three-domain model; Registry datasets are proposed as infrastructure for standardized psychosocial measurement; The paper foregrounds equity through women, ethnic minorities, language, literacy, and socio-gendered inequity; It mentions paediatric and adult cancer care only as analogies for implementation complexity
synthesis_note: This review uses the BPS label mainly to justify implementation of psychosocial assessment and care in orthopaedics. It lists biological, psychological and social predictors of poor recovery, but the analytic work is in psychosocial screening, interventions, workforce and implementation systems. It offers descriptive triadic linkage rather than a three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: BPS functions mainly as intervention rationale and organizing principle. Psychosocial and social content are elaborated, biology is mentioned, and triadic integration is descriptive only.

conceptual_tensions: The paper uses biopsychosocial burden while leaving the model undefined and unmechanized; LBP definitions are inconsistent across included studies; ACR criteria differ across studies and may select more severe FM cases; Measurement heterogeneity and missing minimal clinically important differences limit synthesis; The proposed psychological-to-widespread-pain pathway is explicitly bidirectional and unknown
additional_observations: No formal risk-of-bias or quality appraisal of included studies is reported; Included study designs were mostly cross-sectional, limiting claims about progression from LBP to FM; The search was restricted to English/French publications and three databases; The social domain appears mainly as social support and socioeconomic descriptors, not as a modeled determinant
synthesis_note: The paper operationalizes BPS as a comparative framework rather than an integrated explanatory model. Biological and psychological mechanisms are discussed, especially central sensitization and affect/cognition, but social content is reduced to socioeconomic context and social support.
coding_rationale: Bio and psych are elaborated; social is mentioned. Bio-psych integration is mechanistic; triadic integration is partial because social factors are not tied into the mechanism. Typology is multifactorial.

conceptual_tensions: Small-fiber pathology in FMS is described as unclear in whether it is cause or consequence; The discussion contrasts bottom-up nociceptive amplification with descending inhibitory dysfunction; The threat/soothing model is questioned as possibly just another representation of ANS dysregulation; Intranasal oxytocin for fibromyalgia pain is described as having negative results and limitations; The paper states that whether attachment is key in CSSs and functional somatic disorders remains debated
additional_observations: The article is a narrative/translational pathophysiological model rather than an evidence synthesis; Social content is centered on attachment, caregiving, social support, dyads, and physician-patient relationships rather than work, income, culture, or policy; Clinical translation includes intranasal oxytocin, CT-fiber stimulation, psychoeducation, caregiver participation, and physician-patient relationship work; Developmental scope spans pregnancy, newborns, infancy, childhood, adolescence, and adulthood; The paper uses biomarkers such as HRV, cortisol, IENFD, oxytocin, and inflammatory markers as mechanistic evidence; No formal risk-of-bias or quality assessment is reported
synthesis_note: This narrative/translational paper operationalizes BPS as a neurodevelopmental attachment–CT–oxytocin model of fibromyalgia/CSSs. Biological stress, immune, neural and endocrine mechanisms are elaborated; psychological attachment/affect and social caregiving/social support are integrated, but social content is narrow.
coding_rationale: BPS is explicit but undefined. Biological and psychological content are elaborated; social is mentioned through attachment/caregiving. The triad is mechanistic but narrow.

conceptual_tensions: The paper invokes a BPS interaction but operationalizes it mainly as co-presence of physical and psychosocial components; Social content appears as support or context rather than as a mechanism, despite social functioning and social participation being listed; The review casts older adults as heterogeneous, but the evidence is concentrated in 65- to 75-year-olds; Digital health is framed as improving access, while social support, family/caregiver help, and face-to-face care remain important; Pain outcomes rely on self-report and numeric ratings, while the paper notes subjective interpretation and peak-end bias
additional_observations: The review excludes stand-alone physical and stand-alone psychosocial eHealth interventions, so the BPS frame is enforced at inclusion rather than analyzed as a mechanism; Outcomes are grouped as pain, psychological, physical, integrated biopsychosocial, and other, but pairwise links are mostly listed rather than modeled; eHealth delivery is heterogeneous: web-based programs, mHealth, teleconsulting/video consulting, VR, email, websites, smartphone apps, and wearable activity monitors; No spiritual or existential constructs are named; The article uses QATSDD but not AMSTAR, ROBIS, GRADE, or Cochrane risk of bias; Self-determination needs are named without naming self-determination theory
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mostly as an inclusion criterion for eHealth interventions combining physical and psychosocial components and as an outcome taxonomy. It names biological, psychological, and social content, but social factors are contextual and cross-domain links are mostly listed rather than modeled.
coding_rationale: BPS label frames scope and intervention content; biological, psychological, and social domains are present but parallel, with no specified mechanism, so multifactorial.

conceptual_tensions: Sex and gender are described as distinct but difficult to disentangle in primary pain development; The model integrates biology, behavior, cognition-affect, and sociocultural factors, but mechanisms remain largely unknown; Puberty can be measured as status, timing, or tempo, yet these aspects are often confounded or poorly specified; Sex differences can be quantitative, qualitative, latent, or population-based, but many studies control sex rather than model these types; Pain is framed as primary/nociplastic without peripheral pathology, yet nociplastic processes can amplify nociceptive pain
additional_observations: The paper is explicitly conceptual, not a pooled evidence synthesis, it synthesizes pediatric pain, neuroimaging, and adolescent-development literatures; The BPS frame is operationalized through domain headings and future measurement guidance for puberty rather than through named validated pain instruments; Female puberty, hormones, and CNS development are foregrounded, research on gender-expansive individuals and sex as a continuum is explicitly noted as lacking; The model foregrounds equifinality: no single factor is enough to explain sex differences in primary pain for all youth; Precision-treatment recommendations are made without specifying a concrete multimodal intervention; Many cross-domain claims are framed as hypotheses or gaps, not as tested effects
synthesis_note: This paper operationalizes BPS as a developmental explanatory model for adolescent primary pain: puberty/hormones and CNS are linked with sleep/activity, attention/emotion regulation, and sociocultural exposures to explain female-biased pain. It is integrative but largely hypothetical, with several named gaps and no tested causal model.
coding_rationale: BPS label is explanatory/organizing; all three domains are substantive and linked through puberty/CNS hypotheses, though no formal definition or tested pathway is specified.

conceptual_tensions: FND is described as lacking structural abnormality, yet the review emphasizes network dysfunction and biomarkers; The BPS prism is invoked, but social context is mostly epidemiology, culture, and access rather than an analytic mediator; Psychiatric comorbidities dominate several sections, while somatic and pain comorbidities are presented as overlapping but less developed; FCD is framed as functional despite overlap with dementia and mild cognitive impairment; PRISMA-style selection is used, but the paper states it is not a strict systematic review
additional_observations: The paper uses both biopsychological and biopsychosocial vocabulary; Comorbidity classification is psychiatric versus somatic/medical, not BPS domains; The strongest triadic language appears in the introduction and conclusion, but causal pathways are mostly within bio-psych subdomains; PPPD is the clearest example of a behavioral loop involving vestibular instability, hypervigilance, attentional focus, and cognitive schemas; Future research calls for longitudinal causal studies, biomarkers, and culturally diverse cohorts; No formal BPS definition or operational coding scheme is provided
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly as a broad frame for FND comorbidity rather than a coded model. It substantively covers psychiatric constructs and neurobiological mechanisms, while social content is mostly context, culture, access, and gaps. Cross-domain links are mostly descriptive subtype clustering or care recommendations, with limited explicit three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: Psych-dominant: psychiatric comorbidities and mechanisms receive most detail; neurobiology is developed, social content thinner. BPS is descriptive/integrative in language, not fully mechanistic triad.

conceptual_tensions: The review’s BPS/ICF framing includes social participation, but no included studies assessed it; Physical recovery is the most frequently assessed domain, while functional ability and social participation are underrepresented; Physical activity is protective in some included studies but null or adverse in others; Age thresholds and outcome definitions vary, limiting comparability across studies; Biomedical outcomes dominate despite the stated aim to assess recovery as multidimensional
additional_observations: The ICF framework organizes outcomes into physical, mental, functional, and social participation domains, BPS is not converted into measured variables; Narrative synthesis was used because study heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis; The paper treats lifestyle as a separate category rather than as a pathway linking biological, psychological, and social domains; Quality assessment used NOS and RoB 2, no AMSTAR, ROBIS, or GRADE tool is named; Social support is framed as potentially modifiable, but only one eligible study evaluated it; The paper recommends combining prenatal exercise, mental health support, and workplace adaptations without specifying how these components interact
synthesis_note: The review uses ICF to operationalize a multidimensional recovery frame and groups factors into biomedical, psychological, social, and lifestyle categories. It reports many associations, especially psychological predictors of pain/functional outcomes, but does not define a BPS mechanism or test variables; social participation is absent from included evidence.
coding_rationale: Domains are mostly parallel, with strongest psych-bio and psych-social associations. Social participation is underrepresented. No triadic mechanism is specified.

conceptual_tensions: The paper invokes biopsychosocial dimensions but operationalizes the review mainly through neurobiological mechanisms; AS is defined as auditory/somatosensory acoustic stimulation, yet immersive VR/AR/MR technologies are included because they integrate acoustic information; Acoustic components in immersive technologies are often embedded but not methodologically specified; Evidence is concentrated in perioperative pain, fibromyalgia, chronic back pain, and phantom limb pain, while neuropathic pain is sparse; Multisensory audiovisual interventions raise placebo and blinding concerns
additional_observations: No effect sizes are pooled and no meta-analysis is conducted, the synthesis is narrative despite naming future quality tools; The review includes basic research mechanisms and clinical trials/observational studies across all ages and geographies; Social factors appear mainly as moderators or implementation barriers rather than explanatory mechanisms; Psychological constructs are mostly outcomes or mediators, not a developed analytic domain; The conclusion calls for neuroimaging, biochemical markers, and QST to make mechanisms objective
synthesis_note: This review is a neurobiological narrative review that briefly invokes BPS language but does not operationalize BPS as a three-domain model. It codes acoustic stimulation through CNS, autonomic, immune/endocrine, and neurochemical mechanisms, with psychological constructs mostly as pain/affect outcomes or mediators. Social factors are sparse implementation/contextual moderators, so it exemplifies narrow-despite-label use.
coding_rationale: BPS is explicit but undefined and not used to organize analysis; biological content dominates, psych is present as mechanisms/outcomes, social is thin. Bio-psych integration is mechanistic; triadic integration is only partial.

conceptual_tensions: The abstract presents a systematic synthesis, while the limitations state that the paper is a narrative review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis; The BPS frame promises biological, psychological, and social integration, but the paper is dominated by biological mechanism and treatment taxonomy; CAP is presented as transformative, yet the paper notes it has not been exhaustively studied for pain relief as a primary endpoint; The hippocampus model combines conventional neurobiology with higher-dimensional and Akashic Records language, creating a tension between mechanistic and metaphysical framing; Precision pain medicine depends on biomarkers, but the review states that no single definitive biomarker currently diagnoses pain mechanisms
additional_observations: The paper uses nociplastic pain as a mechanistic category rather than mapping it directly onto ICD-11 chronic primary pain; Psychological constructs are mostly used as therapy targets or risk factors rather than being operationalized through named instruments; Social content is thin and mostly limited to support, stressors, adversity, and broad social determinants; The BPS operationalization is strongest in the nociplastic pain treatment section; CAP and the hippocampus sensor model are original frontiers that may expand the apparent BPS breadth without adding conventional social content; No formal quality or risk-of-bias assessment is reported
synthesis_note: The paper invokes BPS as a broad explanatory frame for chronic pain mechanisms and multimodal care, but operationalizes it mainly through mechanism-based nociceptive/neuropathic/nociplastic taxonomy and biological risk/treatment pathways. Psychological factors are named and used in therapy rationale; social content is thin, mainly support/stressors/social determinants. Triadic integration is mostly co-action/synergy rather than a detailed mechanism.
coding_rationale: BPS language is explicit but mostly organizing/explanatory. Biology is elaborated; psych and social are thinner; lifestyle is developed. Triadic integration is descriptive because synergy is asserted, not fully specified.

conceptual_tensions: The paper argues reciprocal BPS interaction, but the evidence base is mostly cross-sectional or observational, limiting causal inference; All three domains are integrated in synthesis, yet the authors report social determinants and healthcare quality as underexplored; Chronic pain is framed as an ICD-11 diagnostic entity, but included studies vary in operational definitions of chronic pain; Social determinants are central to the BPS account, but included evidence is predominately high-income, limiting transferability; Clinical practice is described as fragmented and pharmacological despite evidence supporting integrated care
additional_observations: The review treats cultural aspects as socially shared meanings and norms, but does not operationalize spirituality or existential suffering; Search terms include nursing diagnostic labels such as impaired sleep pattern, impaired mood regulation, and hypervigilance to pain as sensitizing concepts; Grey literature search yielded no relevant results to be included in the review; The abstract repeats Background and Results paragraphs; SAGER guidelines are used for gender reporting, but no gender analysis tool is named; Quantitative findings are descriptively summarized and mapped to themes, qualitative data are interpretively synthesized
synthesis_note: The paper presents a genuinely integrative BPS account: it synthesizes biological, psychological, social, and cultural determinants and argues reciprocal interaction. However, its operationalization is thematic and narrative rather than measured or causal; social content is acknowledged as underexplored and much evidence is cross-sectional.
coding_rationale: All three domains are substantively present and linked reciprocally in the narrative, so typology is true_integrative. Integration is mechanistic for bio-psych and psych-social through fear-avoidance and support pathways; triadic integration is descriptive because no formal mediator is specified.

conceptual_tensions: The paper rejects the idea that pain is reducible to imaging findings, yet still treats degeneration, arthritis, joints, discs, and neuropathic pain as clinically relevant; It rejects linear movement from biomedical to psychological to social, but much of the text still lists domain examples before explaining integration; It calls for individualized matching to subgroup responses while also emphasizing that trials and care models are heterogeneous and difficult to compare; Pain-modulatory interventions are framed as enabling movement, but efficacy and adverse effects vary across individuals; Communication is treated as treatment, but the paper also identifies time pressure, agenda overload, and the need for structured follow-up as barriers
additional_observations: The paper is a principles-based expert review rather than a formal guideline or evidence synthesis with quality appraisal; BPS is operationalized as clinical principles, not as measured constructs or coded variables; The paper explicitly names patient resources/handouts but does not report validated patient-reported outcome measures; The only named model with explicit cross-domain feedback language is the Pain-Movement Interface; Older adults are treated as a population needing modification of interventions, not as the primary evidence base; The article frames communication as a clinical skill and treatment component
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS as a geriatric clinical-management frame rather than an empirical model: it lists domains, prioritizes patient-centered explanation, expectations, communication, function, and movement, and cites pain-modulatory interventions. Social factors are named as context, but the only triadic integration is a broad feedback-loop narrative.
coding_rationale: BPS functions mainly as a clinical organizing/intervention frame. Psychological content dominates; social content is named but thin; triadic integration is descriptive rather than mechanistic.

bps_operationalization_summary: It operationalizes BPS as a measurement architecture: extracted outcomes include pain intensity, physical health, mental health, quality of life, medication use, and explantation/failure rates, with pain intensity used as comparator. conceptual_tensions: BPS is invoked to justify multidimensional assessment, but no definition, causal pathway, or social mechanism is provided; Pain intensity is criticized as insufficient yet remains the eligibility threshold and comparator outcome; Composite outcomes are proposed as a solution, but the paper states no standardized composite outcome currently exists; Patient satisfaction is described as important but is not clearly represented in the planned extraction domains; Social function and social well-being are named, but extraction focuses on pain, physical health, mental health, quality of life, medication use, and explantation
additional_observations: This is a protocol, all study conduct and synthesis are future-tense; It will extract demographics and country of origin but not social determinants, family, culture, or healthcare access; It will standardize pain intensity to a 0–10 scale for comparison; It proposes meta-analysis with RevMan and Forest plots, but no BPS model is modelled statistically; The BPS frame is measurement-oriented rather than explanatory
synthesis_note: This protocol uses BPS mainly as a justification for composite outcome measures in implantable neuromodulation studies. It names pain intensity, physical health, mental health, quality of life, medication use, and explantation outcomes, with only brief social references. No BPS definition, causal pathway, or social mechanism is proposed; the model is operationalized as a measurement checklist.
coding_rationale: BPS is explicit but undefined. Biological/intervention content is dominant; psychological and social content are named as outcomes only. No cross-domain mechanisms are proposed, supporting pseudo-BPS.

bps_operationalization_summary: Uses BPS as an explanatory and organizing frame, then expands it with minority stress, ecological systems, and intersectionality. It maps structural inequities, psychological distress, coping, and stress physiology to pain and care access. It does not provide a formal measured BPS variable set or empirical test.

conceptual_tensions: The paper frames BPS as foundational but says the model alone is insufficient for TGD youth; The evidence base is described as small, inconsistent, and requiring larger mixed-method trials; Gender affirmation is presented as protective, while binding, hormones, and surgery may also be associated with pain; Tertiary interdisciplinary pain treatment studies represent only youth with access and resources; Policies are described as both barriers to care and targets for advocacy
additional_observations: This is a narrative report rather than a formal systematic review with a transparent search and quality appraisal; Operationalization is conceptual and recommendation-driven, not measured through a formal BPS variable set; Biological content is concentrated in stress physiology, sleep/activity, hormonal regulation, and musculoskeletal effects of binding/surgery; The review’s social/structural domain includes identity, healthcare access, and U.S. policy, not only interpersonal support
synthesis_note: This review uses BPS as an explanatory and organizing frame but expands it with minority stress, ecological systems, and intersectionality. It gives substantive biological, psychological, and social/structural content and proposes cross-domain pathways through stress physiology, cognitive-affective pain mechanisms, coping, and care access. It does not provide a formal measured BPS model or empirical test.
coding_rationale: All three domains are substantive and linked through stress, physiology, coping, and care pathways; triadic integration is mechanistic. Biology is less detailed than psychosocial/structural content, but not marginal.

conceptual_tensions: The paper uses BPS to justify holistic care but never operationalizes body, mind, and environment in extraction or analysis; Existential or spiritual mechanisms for pain reduction are proposed through pain sensitivity and negative evaluation, but no detailed pathway is given; Existentialism is treated as academically labeled, while definitions and related terms such as spiritual, humanistic, and phenomenological approaches may capture different interventions; Spirituality is described as a moderator and intervention theme, but its measurement and mechanism are not specified; The review includes physical functioning and pain outcomes but gives only thin social content, mainly medical system gaps, country, religion, and language
additional_observations: BPS is not used as a coding scheme, extraction fields are intervention details and outcomes; The review treats spirituality as a moderator of existential therapy, not as a social determinant; Included conditions are heterogeneous and mostly not musculoskeletal or neuropathic; The paper names CBT as comparator and adjunct, and suggests combined existential-CBT trials; No quality or risk-of-bias assessment is reported
synthesis_note: This review uses BPS mainly as a holistic rationale for existential/spiritual therapy, not as an operationalized model. It maps existential interventions and pain/mental-health outcomes, with pain sensitivity and negative evaluation as possible pathways and spirituality as moderator; social factors remain contextual.
coding_rationale: BPS is peripheral; biological/psychological/existential content dominate, social content thin; no triadic mechanism, so partial integration and pseudo-BPS typology.

integration_mechanism_summary: PNE is framed to change pain understanding, fear, coping, and self-efficacy, which may reduce pain-related disability and, when combined with exercise, reactivate inhibitory pain processes. PA is described as reducing anxiety/depression/fear and breaking the fear–avoidance cycle. Family involvement is proposed to reduce overprotective responses. No full triadic causal model is specified.

conceptual_tensions: BPS is invoked repeatedly, but the paper does not define it or turn it into coded variables; PNE is framed as part of multidisciplinary biopsychosocial care, yet most measured effects are cognitive, emotional, or behavioral; Pain intensity is treated as a core outcome, but the paper says PNE may work better on cognitive, emotional, and behavioral aspects; Family/caregiver involvement is recommended as important, but only four studies included parents or caregivers; Digital, gamified, and VR delivery formats are promising, but their effectiveness and sustained outcomes remain unclear
additional_observations: The review excludes procedural, oncological, primary neurological condition, and recurrent acute pain; Most included studies were clinical or pilot trials in school/educational settings, one university hospital, one neurology clinic, and two online studies were reported; PNE content was based on international PNE guidelines by Butler and Moseley and Louw and Puentedura; Online cognitive behavioral therapy was a comparator/control in Web-MAP2 studies; Sex/gender is discussed as both biological and sociocultural; Family/caregiver involvement is framed as underused but important for sustainable pediatric chronic pain care
synthesis_note: This pediatric PNE review uses BPS mainly as a practice frame for multidisciplinary care. It extracts PNE effects on pain knowledge, self-efficacy, fear/catastrophizing, function, sleep, parental responses, and some biological markers, but rarely specifies how domains interact. Social content is mostly family/school/system context. BPS is invoked to justify comprehensive care, not operationalized as a three-domain model.
coding_rationale: BPS language mainly justifies multidisciplinary care and multidimensional outcomes. Bio/psych are substantive; social is thinner. Pairwise mechanisms appear, but no full triadic causal model.

conceptual_tensions: BPS acknowledges psychological and sociocultural shaping of pain, yet the review's substantive content is almost entirely neurobiological; Pain is framed as subjective and multidimensional, but operationalized through circuits, receptors, and neuromodulators; Human clinical variability is the target, but much mechanistic evidence comes from rodents; Women are noted as more prevalent in chronic pain, while preclinical studies primarily use male rodents; Neuromodulation is presented as potentially reshaping circuits, but clinical effects are modest or variable
additional_observations: No psychological, social, or BPS construct is operationalized with validated questionnaires in the review; The only social domain content is "sociocultural factors" and insula-related "social behavior"; Personalized pain management is grounded in systems-level neurobiology rather than measured BPS variables; The review treats placebo/nocebo expectations as psychological influences on pain perception but does not analyze them as a framework; The article distinguishes nociception from pain, which counters a common construct conflation; The review cites ICD-11 to frame chronic pain as a disease in its own right
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses the BPS label mainly to frame chronic pain as subjective and variable, but its operational content is a systems-level neurobiology review. It names psychological and sociocultural influences and many bio-psych pathways, yet social factors are not developed or measured and no three-domain mechanism is specified.
coding_rationale: Bio is elaborated; psych is elaborated; social is only mentioned. Bio-psych integration is mechanistic, psych-social none, triadic partial. BPS typology is pseudo_bps.

conceptual_tensions: Sex and gender are explicitly conflated while the review calls for a more nuanced understanding of both; BPS is invoked as operational, but the paper lists factors without formally defining the model or specifying cross-domain mechanisms; Women constitute the majority of CP sufferers, yet research and clinical trials are described as historically male-biased; Sex-specific analgesic and opioid findings are mixed and attributed to differences in experimental design, pain stimulus type, and sample size; Psychological therapy is recommended, but patients may misunderstand it as implying pain is psychosomatic or “in their head”
additional_observations: The review is narrative and expert-driven, with literature critically appraised but no formal risk-of-bias or quality tool named; The paper uses both “psycho-social” and “biopsychosocial,” but the hyphenated psycho-social term is more common in the body; Treatment sections emphasize pharmacology, adverse drug reactions, pharmacokinetics, and sex-disaggregated trial data more than psychosocial care; The paper reports sex-disaggregated prevalence and outcomes but does not pool evidence or provide effect estimates; Lifestyle appears only as a BPS component in the abstract and is not elaborated substantively; Care settings span clinical practice, pain clinics, pain rehabilitation programs, clinical trials, and population surveys
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly by listing sex/gender, biological, psycho-social, and socio-economic factors and organizing evidence into sex-difference sections. It offers several directional associations (SES, mental health, support, treatment response) but little named mechanism. Overall, it is a descriptive true-integrative narrative with bio-psych emphasis and social content mostly as modifiers of care and outcomes.
coding_rationale: Bio and psych are elaborated; social is substantive but thinner. Triadic integration is descriptive, not mechanistic; BPS is used to organize and justify sex-aware care.

conceptual_tensions: Although each disease of this triad could occur in isolation, it is valuable to know whether a single condition increases the risk of the entire triad and whether the rest of PCT needs to be screened for; the survival rate of wounded soldiers has exceeded 90%, but the treatment rate for pain is not as high as the survival rate [ - ]; opioids are the most efficacious agents for acute and chronic pain associated with neurological or tissue injury [ ]; Opioids are not currently recommended as the first treatment for any type of chronic pain in clinical practice, and even many guidelines do not recommend their use in specific populations such as younger groups with non-cancerous pain [ ]; Because neurobiological mechanisms of PTSD are not well established, available pharmacological treatment options are currently limited
additional_observations: PCT, not a formal BPS model, is the paper's main organizing unit; Social content is mostly about work, family burden, VHA/military health systems, and costs rather than social determinants of pain; The BPS label appears only in the abstract and conclusion; The paper's strongest integration is between pain, PTSD/TBI, sleep, cognition, and suicide risk; Interventions span opioids, psychotherapy, rehabilitation, complementary medicine, and shared decision-making; Sleep is treated both as a clinical complication and as a lifestyle/treatment target
synthesis_note: This review treats PCT as chronic pain plus PTSD plus TBI, with biological mechanisms and psychological symptoms developed, social effects as consequences and system burdens. The BPS label is used in the abstract and conclusion to support interdisciplinary, multimodal care, not as an operational framework.
coding_rationale: BPS label is an intervention rationale; bio and psych are elaborated, social is mentioned. Bio-psych mechanisms exist; triadic integration is partial because social factors remain consequences/context.

conceptual_tensions: The paper uses BPS to critique biomedical reductionism, yet its evidence base is narrative and cannot make causal claims; Ethnic disparities are used as explanatory factors, but the paper cautions that individual pain responses remain unique; PNE is framed as promising for reducing opioid dependence, but no statistical analysis or experimental design is included; Provider trust and provider ethnicity are proposed as modulators of pain brain activity, but the review reports this as future research; Social support is treated as important, yet studies disagree and qualitative perspectives are called for
additional_observations: The review includes quantitative, qualitative, and other review articles in its methods; Search terms cover central sensitization, peripheral processing mechanisms, central processing mechanisms, ion channel expression, pain neuromatrix, and graded motor imagery; PNE is consistently framed as adjunctive to physical therapy, especially active movement, GMI, manual therapy, or exercise therapy; OUD is treated as a chronic disorder with physical, social, and mental health implications rather than only a substance-use outcome; Buprenorphine is discussed as affecting depression, anxiety, stress, and quality of life in OUD recovery; The paper calls for fMRI studies comparing PNE and GMI across ethnicities
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS as a systems/ecological rationale for PNE in chronic pain and OUD. It links nociplastic mechanisms, pain beliefs, provider trust, prescribing disparities, and social support, but the integration is narrative and largely cross-domain association rather than tested causal modelling.
coding_rationale: True integrative because all three domains are linked through PNE, pain beliefs, disparities, and neuroplasticity; no formal BPS model is tested.

conceptual_tensions: The paper uses BPS as a broad causal frame but its substantive mechanism is overwhelmingly neurobiological sensitization; It generalizes sensitization from chronic pain to MTBI and PTSD while noting direct evidence is limited or lacking; It searches for biomarkers but concludes that none are definitive, even while arguing for neurobiological underpinnings; The social domain is mostly forensic/legal/secondary-gain content rather than socioeconomic, family, or healthcare-system content; The court context treats chronic pain without tissue damage as controversial despite the article's physiological/neurological framing
additional_observations: Chronic pain is treated as one component of a broader psychological-injury-and-law frame, alongside MTBI and PTSD; The article is a scoping-style literature review of neurobiology rather than a psychosocial intervention review; It names several instruments and diagnostic systems, but they are used conceptually or as cited measures rather than pooled in a meta-analysis; The paper's integration is strongest at neural and cognitive-behavioral levels and thinnest at the social level; The BPS label does explanatory and therapeutic work, but the paper does not operationalize BPS as measured variables or formal constructs; The paper repeatedly distinguishes biological mechanisms from forensic/legal interpretations of psychological injury
synthesis_note: The article uses BPS mainly as a causal scaffold around neurobiological sensitization. Biological content is developed; psychological concepts are linked through reserve/control, fear-avoidance, and attention networks; social content is mostly forensic/legal. It proposes some top-down/bottom-up pathways but not a full three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: Bio-dominant pseudo-BPS: all domains appear, but social/legal factors are thin and triadic reasoning remains partial.

conceptual_tensions: The paper uses BPS language while the social domain remains thin compared with nociplastic neurobiology and fear-avoidance psychology; PRT claims to integrate biopsychosocial approaches but is explicitly described as strongly neurocentric; The paper treats chronic primary pain as without tissue or nerve damage while also requiring careful exclusion of structural, inflammatory, infectious, tumor-related, and neuropathic causes; PRT is presented as promising and guideline-concordant, but the evidence base is described as young, small, and not yet supported by systematic reviews; Implementation in ambulant care is recommended, yet time, resources, therapist training, manuals, and standardized education are named as practical barriers
additional_observations: The first paragraph pairs pain factors as “psychosozial und somatisch”, making the article’s BPS structure a side-by-side opposition rather than a detailed mechanism; The article’s BPS use is strongest as a practical implementation rationale for PRT and weakest as a social determinants framework; Several social elements are embedded in the case example rather than developed as general social mechanisms; The paper’s main pathway is psychological reinterpretation and emotional processing changing brain-generated pain signals; The article treats diagnostic algorithms and structured instruments as ways to identify nociplastic mechanisms rather than as measures of a broad BPS model; The conclusion moves from a specific PRT intervention to a broad paradigm shift toward modern pain medicine
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly as a rationale for implementing PRT in chronic primary/noziplastic pain. It elaborates nociplastic neurobiology and fear-avoidance/self-efficacy processes, links them through central sensitization, neuroplasticity, and the fear-pain cycle, but social content is mostly outpatient care, work/family, stress, and implementation.
coding_rationale: BPS functions mainly as intervention rationale; bio-psych integration is mechanistic, social is thin, triadic integration partial.

conceptual_tensions: Although the paper says different factors interact, it does not specify how biological, psychological, and social factors jointly produce XR response; Neurocognitive functions are central but the paper says they lack consensus definition/use; The transdiagnostic approach seeks shared mechanisms, while pain phenotypes may moderate XR effects; XR is framed as promising, but evidence is preliminary, heterogeneous, and not compared with non-XR cognitive training; Implementation barriers include costs, limited validated games, cybersickness, and lack of protocols
additional_observations: The review is transdiagnostic and explicitly excludes experimental or acute pain; Final synthesis included n = 23 studies; No specific pain, neurocognitive, or psychosocial scale is named, standardized cognitive assessment tools are only recommended; XR is defined as an umbrella term for AR, VR, and MR; The paper recommends reporting frameworks rather than reporting a formal risk-of-bias assessment; The social domain appears mainly through clinical implementation, costs, stakeholders, and policymakers
synthesis_note: This paper operationalizes BPS mainly as a framing and intervention rationale for XR neurocognitive training in chronic pain. It develops neurocognitive/psychological mechanisms and links them to pain, but social content is mostly implementation context. The paper does not provide a full three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: Explicit BPS language is present but not a defined model. Bio-psych pathways are mechanistic; social content is thin; triadic integration is partial because social factors are mostly contextual.

conceptual_tensions: The paper criticizes the biomedical model for ambiguity between pain as alarm, symptom, and disease while also noting that ICD classification may medicalize pain; BPS is credited with integrating biological, psychological, and social factors, but the paper argues it neglects nutrition, lifestyle, environment, and extracellular matrix mechanisms; The proposed functional model is presented as more complete, yet the paper also states that research on it is still in its infancy; Social factors are conceptually recognized in BPS, but the paper says they have received less empirical attention than psychological factors; The paper emphasizes poor correlation between tissue damage and pain perception while also discussing structural lesions as part of biomedical explanations
additional_observations: This is a narrative review, not a systematic review, no formal quality or risk-of-bias assessment is reported; The paper does not empirically operationalize BPS variables through measures, coding, or pooled data; The functional dimension is treated as a fourth dimension added to biological, psychological, and social domains; Most mechanistic claims are citation-based or conceptual rather than tested within the review
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly as a critique of biomedicine and then replaces it with a bio-psycho-functional-social model. Biological/functional mechanisms dominate; psychological and social factors are named and linked to pain, but the paper provides more mechanistic claims for biological terrain and lifestyle/environment than for social pathways. It does not empirically operationalize BPS variables.
coding_rationale: Biological/functional content dominates and is mechanistically developed; psychosocial content is named and linked to pain. The proposed model integrates all domains through matrix/inflammation pathways, so true_integrative despite BPS being critiqued.
